claims.text: Handmade paper is a layer of entwined cellulose fibres, formed by hand sheet by sheet on moulds from fibres suspended in water.

quotes.quote: Handmade paper is a layer of entwined fibres held together by the natural internal bonding properties of cellulose fibres by hand, sheet by sheet on moulds in suspension of fibres in water with or without sizing.
A sheet of paper formed by hand using a mold and deckle is known as handmade paper.

claims.text: Papier-mâché is a composite material of pulped paper mixed with a glue or adhesive paste and other fibrous materials.

quotes.quote: it is a composite material made of pulped paper mixed with a glue or adhesive paste and other fibrous materials

claims.text: Global InCH explains the name papier-mâché as mashed paper, because the objects are built of paper pulp or layers of it.

quotes.quote: However, the craft of papier mache refers, in practice, here actually to the technique of surface decoration rather than the creation of the body of the object.

this technique was also used, particularly during the Mughal period, on doors, panels, palanquins and bedsteads

quotes.quote: The craft is supposed to have come from Kashmir from Central Asia, under King Zain- Ul-Abidin, who invited accomplished artists from Central Asia.

According to Shafi Nagoo the craft can be traced in Kashmir to an Iranian by the name of Torab who came to Kashmir.

claims.text: Papier-mâché is said to have come to India from Samarkand in the time of Timur, in the fourteenth to fifteenth centuries.

quotes.quote: The art of papier-mache is said to have come from Samarkhand to India in the time of Timur Lane, in the fourteenth-fifteenth centuries.

claims.text: Papier-mâché originated in present-day China and was well established in Asia for centuries before it reached Europe in the thirteenth century.

quotes.quote: Its use originated in present-day China, and the technique of crafting objects from it was well-established in Asia over several centuries before being introduced to Europe in the thirteenth century.

claims.text: Global InCH states that Kashmiri papier-mâché is found only in Kashmir district and is practised only by the Shia Muslim community.

quotes.quote: The craft is found only in Kashmir district and is practised only by the Shia Muslim community.

quotes.quote: sakthsazi (mould making, traditionally done by the Sunni Muslim craftspersons - sakhtasaz - located in Naupura) and naqqashi (painting, traditionally done by Shia Muslim craftspersons - naqqash - in Zadibal, Kamangarpura and Hasanabad areas of Srinagar)

claims.text: Kar-i-qalamdani continues to be practised by Shia Muslim descendants of the Persian artists who settled in Srinagar centuries ago.

quotes.quote: This traditional craft continues to be practiced by the Shia Muslim descendants of the Persian artists who settled in Srinagar centuries ago.

claims.text: Papier-mâché is not traditional to West Bengal but has been nurtured in recent years by the Santiniketan school of artists.

quotes.quote: Although the craft of papier mache is not traditional to West Bengal, it has been nurtured over the recent years by the Santiniketan school of artists who have pioneered the craft and passed it on to many artisans.

claims.text: The papier-mâché and clay toy makers of Pondicherry belong to the kuyavar and kosavar community.

quotes.quote: The craftspersons belong to the kuyavar and kosavar community.

claims.text: Kite production in Gujarat dates back to the Mughal empire, with its first centres in Ahmedabad and a craft community called Patangbaaz.

quotes.quote: The craft production of the kites dates back to the historic reign of the Mughal empire. The first centers of production were set up in Ahemadabad. The community of people who indulged in this craft was called Patangbaaz.

claims.text: Jaipur papermakers dip framed wire sieves into the tank of pulped cotton, shake them gently so the fibres interlock, drain the water and sun-dry the sheet.

quotes.quote: Craftspersons dip framed wire sieves into the tank in which the pulped cotton is immersed retaining just the required amount of pulp. Gently shaken the fibres spread evenly and interlock. The water is allowed to seep out and the sheet sun dried.

claims.text: The Encyclopedia of Crafts records that cotton pulping in Jaipur, once arduous hand work, is now semi-mechanised.

quotes.quote: The arduous cotton pulping process earlier done by hand is now semi-mechanised.

claims.text: At Kagazipura, rags and vegetable fibres are soaked overnight and then stirred in a beater with a capacity of about 400 litres.

quotes.quote: The shredders, chindis or canvas rags and vegetable fibers are soaked in water overnight.This soaked mixture is then processed in the beater with a capacity of about 400 liters where it is stirred continuously till it settled down.

claims.text: A wooden frame overlaid with a bamboo or cane mesh is dipped horizontally into the vat, called the hauz, and lifted to gather the pulp.

quotes.quote: A wooden rectangular frame overlaid by a bamboo/cane mesh is dipped horizontally into the Hauz and then lifted gradually upwards until the surface is reached.

claims.text: At Kagazipura each layer of pulp is covered with terrycloth and laid on wooden ply to remove its water, then the sheets are separated by hand and hung to dry for a day.

quotes.quote: The gathered layer of the thin pulp is covered with the terrycloth sheets and these sheets are then transferred on the wooden ply to completely get rid of the water content.
Then each paper sheet is manually separated and they are hung for drying for a day after which, the paper is polished with a machine.

claims.text: In Sikkim, beaten pulp is formed into rectangular sheets, pressed hydraulically, dried and smoothed through a series of hard pressure rollers.

quotes.quote: A pulp is formed as the waste is mixed with water and put into a beater followed by lifting, a process of converting the pulp into rectangular shapes. Water is then removed by hydraulic pressing and individual sheets are left to dry
The final step involves finishing and smoothing the paper through a series of hard pressure rollers.

claims.text: Monpa papermakers scrape and wash off the bark's greenish outer layers to obtain the creamy inner bark, sun-dry it for 2 to 3 days and soak it to soften it.

quotes.quote: By using a knife or dao, the outer greenish/grayish layers of the bark are scrapped and washed with water to remove the scrapped greenish/grayish layers to obtain the whitish creamy inside part of the bark.
The washed bark is then sun-dried for 2 to 3 days and then soaked in water for softening.

claims.text: The boiled bark is beaten to pulp with a wooden hammer on a flat stone, a step called Thungu that compresses the pulp and strengthens the paper.

quotes.quote: On a flat stone plate, the boiled fibers are beaten to a pulp with a wooden hammer locally known as Ruelong.
Beating compresses the pulp, enhances the strength and durability of the paper, and is traditionally referred to as Thungu.

claims.text: Monpa pulp is poured into bamboo frames wrapped with cloth or galvanized net, floated in a water tank and stirred to spread it evenly, and the frames are then sun-dried.

quotes.quote: The fine pulp is then poured into rectangular frames made up of bamboo wrapped with cloth or galvanized net. The frames are then floated in a water tank and stirred continuously for uniform distribution of the pulp over the net.
After some time, the frames are carefully taken out of the water tanks and sun-dried for 2 to 3 h.

claims.text: Making Monpa paper takes about 5 to 7 days, from harvesting the bark to drying the pulp into sheets.

quotes.quote: it takes about 5-7 days for paper production, starting from harvesting of the bark up to dispensing and drying of the pulp to produce paper.

claims.text: Jacquemont saw Kashmiri paper fibres pounded under water-driven wooden stampers at pulp-mills behind the Shalimar Garden, fed by an aqueduct from a Mughal canal.

quotes.quote: Jacquemont observed pulp-mills behind the Shalimar Garden (today Srinagar, Kashmir). An aqueduct supplied the mills with water from a canal built by the Mughal emperors.
the fibres were pounded under water-driven wooden stampers

claims.text: Kashmiri pulp was formed into flat, square, dry cakes and bleached in the sun, then washed in the river and beaten again.

quotes.quote: The resulting slurry in the form of flat, square, and dry cakes was exposed to the sun for bleaching.
The fibres were then washed in the river and beaten again.

claims.text: The Kashmiri paper mould had a rigid wooden frame with crossbars and a movable mat of reeds laced together by a dozen silk threads.

quotes.quote: The first part is a rigid wooden frame made up of four bars mortised at the corners and several triangular-shaped crossbars.
reeds laced together at regular intervals of three or four centimetres by a dozen silk threads

claims.text: Kashmiri sheets were made by dipping the mould twice, so each sheet had two layers of pulp, what is today called a double-dip.

quotes.quote: As a result, the paper sheet was made up of two layers of pulp resulting from the two immersions.
This corresponds to what is called today a 'double-dip'.

claims.text: Wet Kashmiri sheets were applied eight at a time to a wall coated with smoothed plaster, which absorbed the moisture and let them dry gently.

quotes.quote: the sheets were removed from the pile and applied eight by eight to a wall covered with a thin layer of well-prepared and smoothed plaster.
The coated wall absorbed the moisture and allowed the leaves to dry gently.

claims.text: Each dry sheet was rubbed with burnt potter's clay, then sized with rice flour paste applied with a mitt of very hard, thick wool felt.

quotes.quote: first, a rubber armed with a piece of potter's clay, burnt in the fire like a pumice stone, rubbed both sides of each sheet in a brisk movement without pressing hard
The sheet was then passed to the sizer who applied the rice flour paste.
This mitt was made of very hard and very thick wool felt

claims.text: Burnishers rubbed sized sheets on a hard, slightly convex wooden board with a granite pebble and finally with polished jasper or agate.

quotes.quote: Then the sheet was passed to the burnisher who placed it on a board of very hard and highly polished wood, inclined and slightly convex, like a cylindrical surface. He rubbed it hard with a fist-sized granite pebble.
polished it with all his strength but this time with a piece of perfectly polished jasper or agate

claims.text: A Kashmiri sheet could undergo up to eight rounds of sizing and burnishing, and Couvrat Desvergnes sees the paper's quality in this repetition.

quotes.quote: From this description we understand that the quality of Kashmiri paper lies in the repetitive sequences of sizing and polishing. In total, a sheet could undergo up to eight sizing/burnishing iterations.

claims.text: The curved burnishing bench was peculiar to Kashmiri papermaking, as burnishing benches elsewhere in India were flat or concave.

quotes.quote: The curved shape of the burnishing bench is a singularity of the Kashmiri paper technology since other sources and photographs report that the burnishing benches were flat or concave in other regions of India.

claims.text: Kashmiri papier-mâché making is roughly divided between two sets of artists in separate workshops: the sakhtasaz, who process the base material and make the framework, and the naqqash, who design and polish.

quotes.quote: Papier mache making is roughly divided between two sets of artists-sakhtasaz and naqqash. The sakhtasazi artists are involved with processing the base material and preparing the skeleton framework of the craft while the naqqashi artists deal with designing and polishing.
The two sets of artists work in separate karkhanas (workspaces).
Two distinct communities continue to be involved in crafting the kar-i-qalamdani-the sakht-kaz mould-makers and the artists.

claims.text: Sakta makers form papier-mâché objects out of pulp and sell them to the naqqash, the papier-mâché painters.

quotes.quote: There is also a group of people known as sakta makers who 'make papier mache objects out of pulp and sell these objects to the "naqqash" or papier mache painter...'.
The first stage involves the process of papier-mâché moulding, the sakhtsazi, where the shapes of the objects are crafted by the specialist Sakht-kaz community.

claims.text: Sahapedia records that waste paper for Kashmiri papier-mâché is kept in water for five to six days, stretching to 15 in winter.

quotes.locator: In the hands of the sakhtasaz
quotes.quote: Press cuttings, pages from used school notebooks and tissue papers are kept in water for a period of five to six days, stretching to 15 in the winters.

claims.text: Global InCH records that waste paper for Kashmiri papier-mâché is soaked for about a week, then beaten with a big hammer or ground in a limestone mortar.

quotes.quote: Waste paper is soaked in water (usually in a large cauldron or pot) for about a week; the soaked paper is then beaten with a big hammer and/or ground in a maorata made of limestone.

claims.text: Global InCH notes that, unlike in Europe, the paper for Kashmiri papier-mâché is not pulped fully.

quotes.quote: The process is different in Kashmir from that in other European countries in that in Kashmir the paper is not pulped fully.

claims.text: In Kashmiri papier-mâché, layers of prepared paper are patted onto a paper-covered mould, and the thickness of a box comes from using several such layers.

quotes.quote: The mould is first covered with ordinary paper, after which a layer (or several) of the prepared paper is patted on to it.
The thickness of the box (or any other product) is created by using several layers of prepared paper.

claims.text: Global InCH says the Kashmiri papier-mâché article removed from the mould is rejoined with saresh, a thick glue made of natural gum and mishri or sugar.

quotes.quote: The article removed from the mould is re-joined with the help of saresh, a thick glue made of natural gum and mishri or sugar.

claims.text: After the joint is secure, the papier-mâché object is gently rubbed with a wooden file called kathwa.

quotes.quote: After the joint is made secure, the object is gently rubbed with a wooden file called kathwa.

claims.text: The dried Kashmiri papier-mâché form is coated with chalk and glue and smoothed with a baked brick, a step Sahapedia calls gassayiee.

quotes.locator: From the brush of the naqqash
quotes.quote: It is coated with a mixture of chalk mitti (powder) and saresh (a type of adhesive), and polished with a kiln-burnt brick. This process is called gassayiee.
This is followed by a layer of glue and chalk which is painted onto the inside and outside surfaces of the object and then smoothed with a baked brick known as kirkut.

claims.text: Global InCH describes chuna paste made from kurkut, or pumice stone, applied to smooth the surfaces of Kashmiri papier-mâché objects.

quotes.quote: Chuna paste (made from 'kurkut' or pumice stone) is applied to smoothen the surfaces of the product

claims.text: A layer of tissue paper is glued to the smoothed form to make it water-resistant and prevent cracks, before several thick coats of colour.

quotes.locator: From the brush of the naqqash
quotes.quote: Once the piece acquires the desired texture, a layer of tissues is glued to it to make it water-resistant and prevent it from developing cracks. It receives several rounds of gassayiee with sandpaper followed by three or four thick coats of colour.

claims.text: Impart writes that naqqashi begins with a white coat of gypsum and glue, polished with a wet stone once dry until perfectly smooth.

quotes.quote: The naqqashi work begins by coating the surface with a white solution consisting of gypsum and glue. After drying, the surface is further polished with a wet stone until it is perfectly smooth.

claims.text: Global InCH reports that all the painting of Kashmiri papier-mâché, including filling in colours, is done with a brush made of a single cat hair.

quotes.quote: All the painting, including filling in of colours, is done with a brush made of a single cat hair.

claims.text: Impart reports that the freehand designs are made with brushes of Pashmina goat hair and pencils of cat fur.

quotes.quote: On this base, freehand designs are created with brushes created from the hair of Pashmina goats and pencils from cat fur.

claims.text: A final layer of varnish or transparent lacquer seals the paint of a papier-mâché piece, protects the painting and gives it lustre.

quotes.quote: The object is finally finished with a layer of varnish that is applied on top to seal the paint and provide lustre.

quotes.locator: From the brush of the naqqash
quotes.quote: As the paint dries up, various designs are drawn on the papier mache item followed by a layer of varnish to lock the hues.

claims.text: Global InCH says the papier-mâché lacquer is made from the badam tree and must dry naturally, with no heat applied.

quotes.quote: The painter surface is coated with a transparent lacquer made from the badam tree.
The drying process has to be natural; no heat is applied.

claims.text: Sanjhi cutters leave uncut bridges between the cut areas, which form the details of the design and hold the stencil together in one piece.

claims.text: After use, the sanjhi scissors are wrapped carefully in cloth to protect the tip and as a mark of respect to the tool.

quotes.quote: After use, the scissors are wrapped carefully in cloth to protect the tip and as a mark of respect to the tool that creates the Sanjhi.

moment of lifting the Sanjhi is crucial and has to be done in a single movement to ensure that the colours are not disturbed

quotes.quote: The maximum size is 8 feet by 12 feet and the Sanjhi can be octagonal, square, rectangular, or circular.

quotes.quote: in the case of the jal-sanjhi the stencil is placed on still water on which powder, talcum or chalk is sprinkled and then layered with coloured powders

for the year 2015-16 before you

contained two parts of hemp fibres to 16 parts of rags

claims.text: For a floating sanjhi, water is added to an oil-lined dish, and the lighter oil rises to form a film on which the stencil is laid.

quotes.quote: To the oil-lined shallow vessel, water is added. The oil being lighter, floats to the surface and forms an oil film on the water. The stencil is placed on it very carefully and the colours are filled in.

claims.text: A submerged sanjhi is laid with water-insoluble powders on an oil-coated dish, and water is then poured in from the side.

quotes.quote: A submerged Sanjhi is made by taking a shallow dish and coating the inside of the vessel with oil. Powders insoluble in water are used to create the Sanjhi on this oil base by using the cutout patterns.

claims.text: Daphne papyracea is a branched, erect evergreen shrub of the Thymelaeaceae family whose inner fibrous bark is an important source of handmade paper.

quotes.quote: Daphne papyracea Wall. ex G. Don is a branched, erect evergreen shrub belonging to the Thymelaeaceae family.
The inner fibrous bark of the plant is an important source of handmade paper.

claims.text: In Arunachal Pradesh the shrub, locally called Shukshing, is used traditionally by the Monpa of Tawang and West Kameng to make paper.

quotes.quote: In Arunachal Pradesh, the plant is locally known as "Shukshing" and is being used traditionally for making papers by the Monpa tribe of Tawang and West Kameng regions of Arunachal Pradesh.

claims.text: Daphne papyracea grows in cool, lime-free, well-drained sandy loam at 700 to 3,200 m, prefers shade and tolerates temperatures down to -10°C.

quotes.quote: It propagates in cool lime-free well-drained sandy loam, tolerates a dip in temperature up to -10°C, and prefers shady places but grows even in partial sunny places in forested areas (coniferous as well as broad-leaved) at an elevation of 700-3,200 m.

claims.text: Daphne papyracea regenerates if cut 15 cm above the ground and matures within 4 to 5 years for its bark to be harvested for paper.

quotes.quote: D. papyracea can regenerate if cut 15 cm above the ground and mature within 4 to 5 years to harvest bark for making paper.

claims.text: In the traditional Monpa production the researchers observed, mature Daphne papyracea plants aged 5 to 6 years are collected and peeled, and the wood is used as fuel.

quotes.quote: Harvesting or collection: During this step, mature plants aged 5-6 years are collected and peeled off. The bark is collected, and the wood is used as fuel.

claims.text: Maling Gombu says Shugu Sheng takes about three to five years before it can be harvested.

quotes.quote: We are in talks with the forest department about establishing a plantation of the Shugu Sheng shrub to see long term prospects as it takes about three to five years to harvest it

claims.text: Moorcroft alone recorded sunn hemp, Crotalaria juncea, in Kashmiri paper pulp, a species different from true hemp, Cannabis sativa.

claims.text: Sikkim's handmade paper comes from recycled paper and, less often now, the bark of the locally available Argali (Edgeworthia gardenia).

quotes.quote: The basic raw material for the handmade paper stems from two sources - recycled paper and the lesser popular option now, locally available, Argali (Edgeworthia gardenia) bark.

quotes.quote: Handmade paper production excludes wood as a source of fibrous material, utilizes chemical-free approaches, and focuses on drying up the final products using natural renewable sources (sunlight).

claims.text: No trees are cut to make Jaipur's handmade paper, which instead upcycles waste and is strong and durable.

quotes.quote: The product is strong and durable. No trees are cut in its production, instead it upcycles waste.

quotes.quote: It is extremely eco-friendly as it is acid free and consumes less energy and water in comparison to machine made paper.

claims.text: Rather and colleagues cite a documented figure of, on average, 17 trees cut down to produce 1 metric ton of paper.

quotes.quote: It has also been documented that, on average, 17 trees are axed down to produce 1 metric ton of paper.

quotes.quote: D. papyracea is a non-grazing, non-timber forest product (NTFP) and not preferred for regular fuel and found growing well under shade and distributed across 1,800-3,000 m altitude.

claims.text: Distribution modelling found West Kameng and Tawang districts highly suitable habitat for Daphne papyracea in Arunachal Pradesh.

quotes.quote: The best-suited habitat was found in the western parts of Arunachal Pradesh, depicting West Kameng and Tawang districts as highly suitable regions.

claims.text: In a distribution model, the suitable range of Daphne papyracea was largely affected by precipitation and temperature variables, with dry-period precipitation and isothermality the top predictors.

claims.text: Sanjhis are created in autumn, right after the rainy season when the woods are full of flowers, which is why flowers decorate them.

quotes.quote: the superiority in the texture being unquestionable due to the natural abundance of water and to the use of mills moved by streams

lede.text: Paper crafts span making paper by hand, forming entwined cellulose fibres sheet by sheet on moulds from wood-free materials, and making things from paper: papier-mâché from pulp, sanjhi stencils cut from sheets, paper kites, and quilled, folded and layered products.

Handmade paper centres include Sanganer near Jaipur, which lays claim to being India's largest, and Kalpi, while the Monpa of Tawang and West Kameng traditionally made paper from Daphne papyracea bark, a practice now limited to a few households.
Global InCH writes that in Kashmir papier-mâché refers in practice to surface decoration; the work is roughly divided between sakhtasaz, who make the form, and naqqash, who paint it.
Thirukannur Papier Mache Craft, Kashmir Paper Machie, Kalpi Handmade Paper, Arunachal Pradesh Monpa Handmade Paper and Mathura Sanjhi Craft are registered geographical indications.

sentences.text: Handmade paper is a layer of entwined cellulose fibres formed by hand, sheet by sheet, on moulds from fibres suspended in water.
Papier-mâché is a composite of pulped paper with glue or adhesive paste, a name Impart reads as chewed paper and Global InCH as mashed paper.
Global InCH writes that in Kashmir papier-mâché refers in practice to the technique of surface decoration rather than to making the body of the object.
Sanjhi, also called Devasthanakala, is a ritualistic art of fine paper stencilling from Vrindavan and Mathura, linked to the worship of Krishna, and a sanjhi image is deified and worshipped.
The name sanjhi is linked to sanjh, dusk, and also to sajavat, decoration, and sancha, a mould.
Global InCH writes that Gujarat, where kites fill the sky at Uttarayan, is the hub of paper kite production, and that patang is the local word for a kite.
The Monpa handmade paper of Tawang is called Mon Shugu.

Sheets are formed on framed moulds: Jaipur papermakers dip wire sieves into pulped cotton, Global InCH describes a bamboo-mesh frame dipped in the hauz at Kagazipura, Kalpi's GI application has pulp drained by hand onto a metallic sheet, and the Monpa pour pulp into bamboo frames, then float and stir them in water.

In Kashmir the mould was dipped twice, so each sheet held two layers of pulp, and dry sheets were sized with rice flour paste and burnished up to eight times on a convex bench, where benches elsewhere in India were flat or concave.
Kashmiri papier-mâché making is roughly divided between the sakhtasaz, who make the form from pulp, and the naqqash, who paint it, in separate workshops.
In Kashmir, waste paper for papier-mâché is soaked for about a week, or five to six days in another account, then ground in a stone mortar and bound with rice starch.

In Kashmir, layers of prepared paper are patted onto a mould, sawn off when dry and rejoined with a thick glue that one account makes of gum and sugar and another of flour and water, then coated with chalk and glue and rubbed smooth with a baked brick, though Global InCH describes kurkut as pumice stone.

The Tirukanur GI application describes a paste of paper powder, chalk and limestone powders and starch, applied in plaster of Paris moulds cast over clay models, strengthened with pasted paper and dried in sunlight.
Sanjhi stencils are cut with one fine pair of scissors, leaving uncut bridges that form the details and hold the stencil together, and each colour needs its own stencil.

Sources differ on whether a temple sanjhi is still made every evening of Pitra Paksha, only in its final five days in Vrindavan, or only on special occasions, and each is effaced after one day, its material disposed of in the Yamuna.
Plant cell walls are mainly cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, pectin and glycoproteins, and their non-cellulosic glycans shape density, crystallinity and tensile strength.
Glycome profiling found xylan, arabinogalactans and rhamnogalacturonan-I on Monpa paper, correlated with its high tensile strength, and glucose made up 66% and xylose 28% of its glycosyl residues.
Compared with print-copy paper, Daphne papyracea paper showed more cell-wall epitopes, most consistently xylan backbone epitopes.
Monpa papermakers boil cut bark for 3 to 4 hours in ash water; the boiling is meant to remove organic substances, and it softens the bark.
Kashmiri papermakers retted old materials in an alkaline lye of soda ash and lime, and adding sajjī at every washing gave a more refined, homogeneous pulp.
Hard burnishing tightened the grain of Kashmiri paper and thinned each sheet without taking away its weight.
Examined Kashmiri papers measure 0.06 mm to 0.15 mm thick, and the pages of nineteenth-century Kashmiri manuscripts are as transparent and shiny as glass.
Kashmiri paper was strong but thin enough to let sunlight through, and windows were covered with paper in winter.

Daphne papyracea paper has good tensile, double fold, bursting and tearing strength; The Better India reports that Mon Shugu lasts much longer than conventional paper, and Maling Gombu, a Tawang-based social worker, says it is 80 percent stronger in tensile strength.
Floating and submerged sanjhis rely on oil, lighter than water, and on powders insoluble in water.
Handmade papers are traditionally made from wood-free materials such as cotton, silk cotton, banana fibres, kenaf, bagasse and agricultural wastes.
Jaipur paper is largely made of cotton rags left from the garment trade, Sanganeri paper also uses silk, banana trunk fibres and petals, and khadi paper is made from khadi rags.
The KNHPI's 2015-16 annual report named cotton hosiery waste as the raw material of the Indian handmade paper industry and said it was scarcely available and getting costlier.
In 1831 Kashmiri paper was made from worn cloth, rags, ropes and sacks, with tát canvas bags giving the best quality, and a 1908 recipe used rags, hemp, sajjī, lime and rice flour.
Kashmiri paper stood out for its fineness, whiteness and extreme polish, and Daulatabad paper became famous for its glossiness and durability.
Daphne papyracea fibres are thicker and longer than rice straw, sugarcane or bamboo fibres.

In Kashmir, papier-mâché pulp is bound with rice starch and moulds once of clay are now of wood, brass, metal or plaster of Paris; two craft accounts add copper sulphate to the pulp, and Global InCH's western Rajasthan papier-mâché uses waste paper and clay.
Global InCH reports that Kashmiri papier-mâché colours came from walnut skins, saffron and indigo, with white lead and lapis lazuli imported, before synthetic poster and water colours replaced them.
Jaipur lays claim to being the largest centre of hand papermaking in India, with its production cluster centred on Sanganer.
Monpa papermaking became part of local custom and culture in the West Kameng and Tawang regions of Arunachal Pradesh.
Kalpi in Jalaun is recognized for handmade paper manufacturing, but sources differ on whether papermaking there is an ancient craft or was introduced by Munnalal 'Khaddari', a Gandhian, in the 1940s.

Global InCH writes that nearby lakes gave Daulatabad the abundant water and space that handmade papermaking needs, and Baden Powell credited the texture of Kashmiri paper to abundant water and mills moved by streams.

Sanjhi originated in Vrindavan and Mathura, two virtually contiguous towns on the Yamuna in the region of Vraja, artisans also practise it in Alwar, and the EZCC book links the temple sanjhis of Nathdwara in Rajasthan to those of Vrindavan.
Global InCH names papier-mâché centres in Gwalior, Ujjain, Indore and Harda, in Bharatpur, Ajmer, Palai and Jaipur, and in Kosapalayam near Pondicherry.
Global InCH names Gujarat the largest hub of kite production, with Vadodara, Surat and Ahmedabad known for their kite markets.
Kashmir Life names Ganderbal and Nowshehra the two main bases of Kashmiri papermaking, and Couvrat Desvergnes places its pulp-making in hamlets along the Sindh River, one of them clearly Ganderbal.
In a distribution model, the suitable range of Daphne papyracea was largely affected by precipitation and temperature variables.
Sanjhis are created in autumn, right after the rainy season, when the woods are filled with flowers.
In Kashmir, papier-mâché forms take longer to harden in winter, when bukhari heaters are installed in the workshops.
Global InCH reports that Kagazipura's water resources have depleted and the area has become semi-arid and arid.

Rather and colleagues write that handmade paper production excludes wood as a fibre source, uses chemical-free approaches and dries products in sunlight, though Kalpi's GI application has rags beaten to pulp with water and chemicals.
No trees are cut for Jaipur's paper, which upcycles waste, and Global InCH calls Rajasthan's handmade paper acid free and lower in energy and water use than machine-made paper.
Rather and colleagues cite a documented figure of, on average, 17 trees cut down to produce 1 metric ton of paper.
Daphne papyracea is a non-timber forest product that is not grazed, and modelling found West Kameng and Tawang districts highly suitable habitat.
Daphne papyracea, locally called Shukshing, is an evergreen shrub of the Thymelaeaceae family whose inner bark the Monpa use for paper.
It grows in cool, lime-free, well-drained sandy loam and tolerates temperatures down to -10°C, at elevations given both as 700 to 3,200 m and as 1,800 to 3,000 m.
Sources differ on its harvest age: it regrows for harvest within 4 to 5 years, plants aged 5 to 6 years are collected, and Maling Gombu gives about three to five years.
Kashmiri pulp used hemp, and Moorcroft alone recorded sunn hemp, Crotalaria juncea, a species different from true hemp.
Global InCH writes that Sikkim's handmade paper comes from recycled paper and, less often now, the bark of the locally available Argali.
Sources differ on when papermaking reached India, from the 3rd century BC to the tenth century, when it is believed to have come with invading armies and settlers, or the 11th century.

The Kagzi papermakers came to Sanganer, but sources differ on whether Raja Man Singh in the 16th century, Sawai Jai Singh II, or Raja Man Singh II in 1728 brought or patronised them, and the KNHPI traces the community's history to the 14th century.
Handmade paper suffered under British rule, Gandhi bought it in bulk for his Ashram, KVIC took it up after independence and the KNHPI arose at Sanganer in 1991.

Couvrat Desvergnes writes that Sultan Zayn al-ʿAbidīn invited craftsmen to Kashmir in the middle of the fifteenth century and the first paper-mill stood in a royal garden of Srinagar, while Kashmir Life gives the 14th century and Impart has Kashmiri paper sought after in the thirteenth.
Jacquemont's 1831 account is the earliest of Kashmiri papermaking, which declined from the second half of the nineteenth century until Hunter found its paper-makers in poverty in 1937.

Monpa papermaking originated over 1,000 years ago and is historically linked to Buddhist practice; a 2020 government release says the Monpa once sold their paper to Tibet, Bhutan, Thailand and Japan, and the craft almost disappeared in the last 100 years.

Kashmiri papier-mâché takes its name, kar-i-qalamdani, from pen cases, and sources differ on its origin, from artists of Persia or Central Asia invited by Zain-ul-Abidin, it is believed, to an Iranian named Torab.

Sources differ on when sanjhi began, from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries or the 16th and 17th centuries to the seventeenth-century temple tradition of Vrindavan, which is now rare and seems confined to a few temples at Vrindavan and Barsana.
In 2015-16 the KNHPI called handmade paper a tiny industry, 0.055 to 0.14% of India's paper and board, heavily dependent on the foreign market.

The KNHPI saw a definite decline in the handmade paper industry, though its output grew 41% from 5,100 MT in 2014-15 to 7,200 MT in 2015-16, and exports rose from Rs 53 crores to Rs 60 crores after a very bad phase of 7 to 8 years.

Kashmir Paper Machie (certified 2012), Thirukannur Papier Mache Craft (2011), Kalpi Handmade Paper (2023), Arunachal Pradesh Monpa Handmade Paper and Mathura Sanjhi Craft (both 2024) are registered geographical indications, and Gwalior Papier Mache Craft was certified in 2025.
KVIC launched a Monpa handmade paper unit in Tawang to revive the craft and train local youth.
In 1831 the Srinagar paper-mill Jacquemont visited worked only eight months a year, its burnishers earning 3 annas a day, and a dastā of average paper sold for 0.75 to 0.80 francs.
The hand-cut sanjhi stencil, once a tool of the trade, has become the final product, made into lampshades, notebooks and wall decorations.
Sakht-kaz mould-makers face difficulties from a lack of innovation in shapes and a need for better mould-making technology.

GI Journal 170 of 13 February 2023 describes Kalpi's handmade paper cluster as engaging more than 5000 craftsmen and approximately 200 units, and Rather and colleagues reported Daphne papyracea paper sold at INR 22 per piece in 2022.
Jaipur handmade paper ranges from white to rainbow colours, with leaves, grass, petals, silk thread and tinsel embedded.
Kashmiri papier-mâché motifs such as the hazara, gul andar gul and chinar keep their Persian names, and many papier-mâché artworks carry designs also found in shawls, carpets and woodwork.
A pattern done only in gold leaf is called sonposh, and Global InCH calls the box the ubiquitous Kashmiri papier-mâché product.

Global InCH records that in Patna, Saraikella, Hazaribagh, Murhu, Khunti and Madhubani, Chhau dance masks, once of wood and then bamboo, are today of papier-mâché, and in some hereditary mask-making families only dancers are allowed to make them.
Sanjhi motifs come from the Krishna legend and scenes of Vrindavan, later broadened with Mughal jali patterns, and some stencils drew on Mughal geometric designs.
Through the concept called chaski, a sanjhi composition is divided into smaller units so that different colours can fill its parts.
Global InCH writes that in Gujarat the kite, first prism-shaped, is now commonly quadrangular for better mobility and control.
Global InCH writes that folding, cutting, dyeing, recycling, layering and quilling have multiplied paper products.
